  "response": "# Erdős Problem 99: second-order Farkas deformation test

Research assessment — 29 October 2026

## 1. Main findings

Erdős Problem 99 remains open. The second-order Farkas approach yields a valid deformation criterion, but the square and the globally optimal eight-point regular-heptagon configuration expose a fundamental limitation: the relevant quadratic stress form vanishes on every admissible first-order velocity in both examples.

The independent mathematical findings are:

1. A rigorous second-order Farkas lemma is available. It characterizes when a prescribed first-order velocity can be completed by a second-order acceleration to give strict feasibility and a quadratic decrease in diameter. The decisive condition involves every nonzero nonnegative equilibrium stress supported on the neutral constraints, not merely one selected KKT stress.

2. The four-point square passes the test without revealing a triangle. Its positive stress forces every admissible first-order velocity to be a rigid-body velocity. The quadratic form QQQ is identically zero on these velocities, even though the square is an exact, triangle-free global optimizer.

3. The globally optimal eight-point heptagon-plus-center has an explicit triangle-sensitive deformation. Holding the seven outer vertices fixed and moving the eighth original point along a particular radial segment produces a continuous family of exact global optimizers. Every configuration before the endpoint is triangle-free; the endpoint contains an original unit equilateral triangle. Throughout this family, the optimal diameter is unchanged.

4. The second-order obstruction cannot detect this transition. At the centered heptagon, the interior point belongs to no active contact or diametral constraint. Consequently, its velocity is invisible to the equilibrium stress and QQQ. At the triangle-containing endpoint, the newly created interior contacts necessarily have zero equilibrium-stress coefficients.

These are finite-dimensional structural results, not an asymptotic resolution. They do not prove or disprove the eventual assertion that every unrestricted exact global optimizer contains an original unit triangle.

The original problem statement explicitly remains classified as open. Bezdek and Fodor's 1999 paper supplies the exact global n=8n=8n=8 diameter used below. The second-order duality is closely related to established tensegrity rigidity theory, particularly Connelly and Whiteley's work; I do not claim originality or mathematical priority for that general principle. Erdős Problems+2

### Two important corollaries

Corollary 1 — necessary condition for any C2C^2C2 deformation.

If a C2C^2C2 path with initial velocity uuu satisfies the original separation conditions and

diam⁡(P(t))2≤D2−κt2,\operatorname{diam}(P(t))^2\le D^2-\kappa t^2,diam(P(t))2≤D2−κt2,

This follows by replacing the strict inequalities in (4) with non-strict inequalities and summing them against the stress coefficients. The acceleration terms cancel by equilibrium.

In particular, one stress violating (9) rules out every such C2C^2C2 path with that specified initial velocity.

Corollary 2 — second-order obstruction at an exact global optimizer.

Suppose in addition that PPP is an exact global minimum-diameter configuration. Then for every first-order feasible uuu, there exists a nonzero nonnegative neutral equilibrium stress satisfying

Qu(α,β)≤0.(10)\boxed{Q_u(\alpha,\beta)\le0.} \tag{10}Qu​(α,β)≤0.​(10)

∑NCαij=D2∑NHβij.(11)\sum_{N_C}\alpha_{ij} =D^2\sum_{N_H}\beta_{ij}. \tag{11}NC​∑​αij​=D2NH​∑​βij​.(11)

Every nonzero nonnegative stress therefore has ∑βij>0\sum\beta_{ij}>0∑βij​>0. Normalize by ∑βij=1\sum\beta_{ij}=1∑βij​=1. Equation (11) bounds all coefficients, so the normalized stress set is compact.

Both conclusions contradict exact global optimality. Hence (10).

This necessary condition does not assert that one universal stress works for every velocity: the stress may depend on uuu. Nor does Q=0Q=0Q=0 establish the existence or nonexistence of a nontrivial deformation. Higher orders may matter.

## 7. Can a nonlocal exchange rescue the triangle argument?

The examples identify the precise obstruction.

A nonlocal exchange theorem strong enough to settle the original conjecture would need to establish, for all sufficiently large nnn, something beyond equilibrium—such as a strict diameter reduction whenever an exact global optimizer has no unit triangle.

The heptagon demonstrates why the conclusion cannot follow from stress positivity and diameter pins alone. There are two globally optimal configurations with the same outer hull, one triangle-free and one triangle-containing.

The infinite polygon family demonstrates why an argument based solely on the algebraic stress equations cannot distinguish a large non-global stationary cycle from a genuinely optimal packing.

The convex-hull result gives a further limitation: in global configurations, diameter pins occupy only O(n)O(\sqrt n)O(n​) boundary sites. Any argument intended to force interior unit triangles must explain how boundary pinning constrains bulk contacts, including possible stress-free sectors.

## 8. Adversarial checks and unresolved gaps

Does the polygonal-hull theorem prove the conjecture?

No. It constrains the number of extreme sites but places no lower bound on the number of unit triangular faces. A configuration can have many convex-hull vertices and no unit equilateral triangle.

Not for a fixed nontriangular angle once nnn is sufficiently large; inequality (6) applies to every finite subset. But it does not rule out an angle tending to 60∘60^\circ60∘ or 120∘120^\circ120∘.
